sequence_index values are drawn from the private band 1200-1299 and are ordered so that every point follows everything it depends on. The post-merge renumbering pass re-seats them into 1..154.

gr_used_to declares confusion_set cs_past_habit and is currently its only member in this block: the closed 154-id set contains no choice-role point for past habit, so the set has no board_id owner. Flagged for the verify agent.
The doubled past marker after did ("did you went") is coded word_form_wrong; the 53-code taxonomy has no dedicated slug for marking the past twice.

points.title: Saying what someone or something was like at a time that is over

teach.can_do: I can say what someone or something was like at a time that has finished.
teach.why_it_matters: Every past story opens with the scene, and the scene needs was or were. Pick the wrong one and the slip sits in your first sentence.
teach.meaning: Most verbs tell you what somebody did. Be does a different job: it says what somebody or something is like, or where it is. Was and were do that same job at a time that has already closed. They park a description in the past and leave it there. The sentence tells you how things stood then, and it makes no claim at all about how they stand today.

form.pattern: I / he / she / it + was  ·  you / we / they + were
notes: One person or one thing takes was; more than one takes were
you takes were whether you are talking to one person or to twenty
In speech the vowel almost disappears: was and were come out short and flat
form.negative: was not / wasn't  ·  were not / weren't
form.question: Was I ...?  /  Were you ...?

marks.label: the sentence says nothing about here

spec.caption: These two words do not report an action. They hold a description still, at a moment that has passed.

worked_example.sentence: The lifts in the Brackenfield flats were out of order for most of January.
worked_example.why_this_form: There is more than one lift, so the description takes were, and January has closed, so the description stays back there with it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Are would drag the broken lifts into today and turn an old complaint into a live one the reader has to act on.

notice_set.sentence: The two coaches were late and the whole group missed the ferry.
notice_set.question: How many coaches is the speaker talking about?
notice_set.why: Were goes with more than one thing, and here it is the coaches it belongs to.

notice_set.sentence: My grandmother was a cook in the harbour hotel.
notice_set.question: Does she work there today?
notice_set.why: The description is parked in a stretch of time that has closed. What she does now is outside what the sentence claims.

notice_set.sentence: You were the first one at the gate.
notice_set.question: Could the speaker be talking to just one person?
notice_set.why: You takes were whether it is one person or a whole crowd, so were tells you nothing about the number here.

notice_set.sentence: The kitchen was cold and the back window was open.
notice_set.question: What would you have seen if you had walked in?
options: A room in a certain state
notice_set.why: Nobody does anything in this sentence. It hands you a picture of how the room stood.

notice_set.sentence: Weren't the roads closed that weekend?
notice_set.question: Does the speaker already think the roads were closed?
notice_set.why: A question shaped like this one is a way of checking something the speaker already believes.

teach.rule_line: One thing takes was. More than one takes were, and so does you.
teach.false_rule: That were always signals more than one. You were is a single person half the time, and that is the commonest slip in the whole unit.

errors.wrong: The two lifts in the block was out of order all week.
errors.right: The two lifts in the block were out of order all week.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reaches for was because it is the form they met first and the one they hear most. Nothing in the sentence forces them to look back at what the description belongs to.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: was becomes were.
errors.l1_note: Many languages do not change the verb for one or many, so there is nothing to transfer.

errors.wrong: The box of tools by the back doors were heavy.
errors.right: The box of tools by the back doors was heavy.
errors.why_it_happens: Tools and doors sit right next to the verb and both are more than one, so the ear picks were. The thing being described is the box, four words earlier.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: were becomes was.

errors.wrong: You was at the gate before me.
errors.right: You were at the gate before me.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is talking to one person, counts one, and takes the one-thing form. You is the exception and nobody ever tells them.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: was becomes were.

pays_in.note: Every long turn about a past occasion opens by setting the scene.
pays_in.model: The hall was freezing and the seats were all wooden, so nobody wanted to sit down.

pays_in.note: Describing a chart of past years is one long stretch of was and were.
pays_in.model: In 2016 the coastal routes were the busiest in Norland, and rail freight was a long way behind.

pays_in.note: Both words are said fast and flat, and wasn't is often a single sound.
pays_in.model: The office wasn't open, so we waited outside with the boxes.

used_in.quote: The card asks what the thing was like before it asks what you did with it, and that first half is built entirely out of these two words.
Every figure on the graph belongs to a year that has closed, so every sentence about it needs one of these two.

payload.sentence: The twins were in the same class until the summer.
payload.question: How many children is the speaker talking about?

feedback.why_key: Were belongs to the twins, and it is the form English keeps for more than one.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the small word before the description; it counts for you.

payload.sentence: The list of repairs from the two upstairs flats was on the desk all week.
payload.question: How many lists were on the desk?

feedback.why_key: Was belongs to the list, not to the flats sitting next to it, so there is one list.
feedback.feed_forward: Find what the description is about before you count.

items.decision_cue: You was

payload.context: Two cousins are arguing about who arrived first.
payload.sentence: You was in the car park when I got there.
reasons: you always takes were, even for one person
the speaker means more than one person
the gate was not open
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: You is the exception. It takes were whether it points at one person or at a room full of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Say you were out loud until it is the only thing that sounds right.

payload.context: From a note on last year's harbour survey.
payload.stem: The two coast routes ___ (be) busier in July than in any other month.

feedback.why_key: Two routes are being described, so the description takes the more-than-one form.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the thing being described, then choose.

payload.context: Halina is describing the flat she grew up in.
payload.stem: The noise from the goods trains ___ (be) worse in the summer.

feedback.why_key: One noise is being described. The trains are only where it came from.
feedback.feed_forward: Ignore the words between and look back at what is being described.

payload.given: The stairwell was dark. The two landings were dark as well.
payload.instruction: Put both facts into one sentence that begins with the stairwell.
payload.starter: The stairwell and the two landings ___

feedback.why_key: Once the two are joined, the description covers three things at once and takes were.
feedback.feed_forward: Join the two things first, then choose the form.

payload.audio_text: We weren't ready and the changing rooms were still locked.

expected: we weren't ready and the changing rooms were still locked
we werent ready and the changing rooms were still locked
we were not ready and the changing rooms were still locked

feedback.why_key: Weren't is one quick sound in speech. If you never hear it you will never write it.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the short flat word before the description.

payload.context: Build one sentence describing a college hall early in the morning.

expected: the hall was empty and the side doors were open

feedback.why_key: Two descriptions sit side by side, and each one takes the form that matches what it belongs to.
feedback.feed_forward: Match each description to its own thing before you join them.

items.decision_cue: The cost of the two new ferries

payload.context: From a report on harbour spending in Norland.
payload.sentence: The cost of the two new ferries were higher than the council expected.
reasons: the description belongs to the cost, and there is one cost
there were not two ferries
the council expected nothing at all
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Ferries is the nearest word but it is not what the sentence is describing. One cost was higher.
feedback.feed_forward: Put your finger on the thing being described before you decide.

payload.sentence: My parents was both at the harbour that morning, so nobody was at home.

feedback.why_key: The second half is right: nobody counts as one. The first half describes two people.
feedback.feed_forward: Check each description against its own thing, not against the sentence.

items.decision_cue: The lifts were out of order.

payload.context: Two tenants describing the block they lived in.
sentences: The lift was out of order.
The lifts were out of order.
meanings: The block has one lift and nobody could use it.
The block has more than one lift and none of them worked.

feedback.why_key: One letter on the thing, one word on the description, and the size of the problem doubles.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the description and the thing together as one unit.

payload.prompt_text: Think about the home you lived in when you were ten. Write one sentence describing two things in it — not what anybody did there, only how things stood.

feedback.why_key: A description of a finished time needs no action in it at all, and the two things you name decide the two forms.
feedback.feed_forward: Describe, do not narrate; check each form against its own thing.

payload.prompt_text: You have two minutes on the card The first phone or computer you owned. Open with two sentences that say what it was like, before you say anything you did with it. Ninety seconds to plan.

feedback.why_key: An examiner hears the scene before the story, and the scene is carried entirely by these two words.
feedback.feed_forward: Set the scene in two sentences, then start the story.

points.title: Saying that something happened and finished, using the -ed ending

teach.can_do: I can say that something happened and is over, using the -ed ending.
teach.why_it_matters: This ending is how English says the thing is done. Leave it off and every sentence you write drifts back into today.
teach.meaning: Adding -ed to a verb makes one claim and one only: this happened, and the happening is behind us. It does not say how long it took, whether it happened once or forty times, or whether anybody can still see the result. It marks the whole thing as closed. English puts that mark on the verb, once, whether or not the sentence ever says when.

notes: A verb already ending in e just adds d: close → closed
A consonant plus y turns into ied: study → studied, carry → carried
One short vowel and one final consonant doubles it: stop → stopped, plan → planned
Three sounds, one spelling: worked ends in a t sound, filled in a d sound, and wanted adds a whole extra beat
form.negative: did not walk / didn't walk — the ending comes off, because did is now carrying it (unit point four)
form.question: Did you walk ...? — again the plain verb, because did has taken the job

marks.label: the sentence stops well short of here

spec.caption: The ending puts a lid on the event. Nothing about today is being claimed.

worked_example.sentence: The college moved its evening classes to the harbour campus.
worked_example.why_this_form: The move happened and finished. One ending on one verb tells the reader that, without any date being named at all.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Moves would turn it into something the college does again and again, as a matter of policy, and would say nothing about any particular move.

notice_set.sentence: The library closed at four during the exam weeks.
notice_set.question: Does the library still close at four?
notice_set.why: The ending shuts the whole thing away in a finished stretch of time. Today is not part of the claim.

notice_set.sentence: We walked to the study group together.
notice_set.question: Did this happen once, or many times?
notice_set.why: The ending says finished, not how often. Only extra words can tell you that.

notice_set.sentence: The tutor emailed the results and everybody opened them at once.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Two closed events, told in the order they happened. English lets the order of the words do that work.

notice_set.sentence: She wanted a place on the course.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker say whether she got one?
notice_set.why: The ending closes the wanting. What came after it is a different sentence.

notice_set.sentence: The two colleges shared a library for years.
notice_set.question: Do they share it now?
notice_set.why: Closing the years off is a way of saying the arrangement is over. If it were still running the speaker could not have shut it.

teach.rule_line: If it happened and it is over, put -ed on the verb, once.
teach.false_rule: That you only need the ending when the sentence names a time. Most past sentences name none, and the ending goes on anyway.

errors.wrong: I joined the study group and we walk to the library every Thursday.
errors.right: I joined the study group and we walked to the library every Thursday.
errors.why_it_happens: The first verb was chosen carefully and the second was not. Every Thursday feels like a habit, and habits pull the speaker back into the present without warning.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: walk becomes walked.

errors.wrong: The bus stoped outside the college gates.
errors.right: The bus stopped outside the college gates.
errors.why_it_happens: The rule the learner has is add -ed, and it is the right rule. The doubling is a spelling habit nobody mentions until it is already wrong on paper.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: stoped becomes stopped.

errors.wrong: We studyed the same subject for two years.
errors.right: We studied the same subject for two years.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner applies the ending exactly as taught. Nothing in add -ed warns them that a consonant plus y behaves differently.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one letter: the y becomes an i.

errors.wrong: The course started in October. It lasts ten weeks and finished before the holiday.
errors.right: The course started in October. It lasted ten weeks and finished before the holiday.
errors.why_it_happens: Facts that are still true about the course, like its length, feel present to the writer even inside a report about a course that has ended.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one letter: the s becomes a d.

pays_in.note: Any example from your own experience is written in this form from start to finish.
pays_in.model: When the council opened the riverside path, local shops reported far more passing trade.

pays_in.note: The long turn is almost always a story, and a story runs on this ending.
pays_in.model: I signed up for the evening class and travelled across town twice a week for a year.

pays_in.note: The ending is often a single consonant and it is easy to miss entirely.
pays_in.model: They finished the survey and posted the results to every household.

used_in.quote: A skill you learned outside school is a finished story, and every sentence in it carries this ending.
Every year on the graph has closed, so every movement described in the answer is reported with this form.

payload.sentence: The college opened a second entrance on the harbour side.
payload.question: Is the opening still to come?

feedback.why_key: The ending puts the whole event behind the speaker. Nothing about it is still waiting to happen.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the ending as a lid on the event.

payload.sentence: I walked to my classes.
payload.question: Where does this sit?
options: a closed stretch of the past
a habit the speaker still has

feedback.why_key: The ending shuts the habit away. Whether the speaker still walks is a separate sentence they have not said.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the event on the line before you think about now.

items.decision_cue: and we travel to the coast

payload.context: From a paragraph about the writer's first year at college.
payload.sentence: I signed up for the field trip and we travel to the coast together.
reasons: the second verb slipped back into today
the writer did not join the group
a group cannot walk anywhere
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Both events belong to the same closed year. One of them has been left standing in the present.
feedback.feed_forward: Read your verbs on their own, in order, before you move on.

payload.context: From a short report on an evening course.
payload.stem: Twenty-two students ___ (enrol) in September and eighteen finished the year.

feedback.why_key: One short vowel and one final consonant, so the consonant doubles before the ending.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the verb aloud and listen for a short vowel before you spell it.

payload.context: From a note on a walking scheme in Ashfield.
payload.stem: The clinic ___ (copy) the results to the council before the deadline.

feedback.why_key: A vowel before the y keeps it; a consonant before the y turns it into an i.
feedback.feed_forward: Look at the letter before the y, then spell the ending.

payload.given: The tutor emails the reading list and the students print it in the library.
payload.instruction: Move the whole sentence into a term that has ended.

expected: emailed the reading list and the students printed it in the library

feedback.why_key: Two verbs, two endings. Moving one and leaving the other is the commonest way this goes wrong.
feedback.feed_forward: Change every verb in the sentence, not the first one.

payload.audio_text: They finished the project and waited for the marks.

expected: they finished the project and waited for the marks

feedback.why_key: One ending is a single hiss at the end of a word; the other adds a whole beat. Same spelling, two sounds.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the end of each verb, not the middle.

payload.context: Build one sentence about work that was completed in Verdon.

expected: the council planted four hundred trees along the river path

feedback.why_key: The ending sits on the verb and nowhere else, right after the thing that did it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the doer first, then the verb with its ending.

items.decision_cue: The college closes on the first Friday of every month.

payload.context: Two lines taken from different college notices.
sentences: The college closes on the first Friday of every month.
The college closed on the first Friday of every month.
meanings: This is the arrangement now, and you can plan around it.
That was the arrangement during a stretch of time that has ended.

feedback.why_key: One ending is the whole difference between a notice you can act on and a fact about a past year.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the arrangement is still running.

payload.sentence: We applyed for the same course and both of us started in the autumn.

feedback.why_key: The rest of the sentence is fine. A consonant sits in front of the y, so the y cannot stay.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the letter before a final y before you add the ending.

items.decision_cue: It runs for ten weeks

payload.context: From a report on a walking scheme that ran two winters ago.
payload.sentence: The scheme opened in October. It runs for ten weeks and reached four hundred households.
reasons: one verb in the middle is still standing in the present
the scheme never started
ten weeks is too long for a scheme
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The length of the scheme feels like a permanent fact, so it escapes the closed stretch the other two verbs are in.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the middle verb of a paragraph twice; it is the one that slips.

payload.prompt_text: A course or class you signed up for and completed. Write one sentence with two verbs in it, saying what you did and what happened next.

feedback.why_key: Two closed events in one sentence is the smallest piece of a story, and both of them need the ending.
feedback.feed_forward: Write it, then check both verbs before you submit.

payload.prompt_text: Take the example paragraph from your last Task 2 answer and rewrite two sentences of it so that the example is clearly a finished case rather than a general habit. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: An example only counts as evidence once the reader can see it actually happened and finished.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn the general claim into one thing that happened.

points.title: Using the past of the verbs that refuse the -ed ending

teach.can_do: I can use the past of the common verbs that do not take the -ed ending.
teach.why_it_matters: The verbs that break the rule are the ones you need most: go, take, make, buy, eat. Every second sentence of a story leans on one of them.
teach.meaning: About ninety everyday verbs do not build their past by adding anything. They swap to a different word: go becomes went, buy becomes bought, eat becomes ate. The meaning is exactly the meaning of the -ed ending — it happened, it is closed — but the shape has to be learned one verb at a time. There is no rule waiting to be discovered here. There is a list, and it is short, and you already know half of it.

form.pattern: a separate past word, learned verb by verb  (go → went · buy → bought · eat → ate)
notes: Learn them in sound families rather than alphabetically: bring/brought, buy/bought, think/thought
A second family swaps one vowel: drink/drank, sing/sang, begin/began
A third family does nothing at all: cut/cut, put/put, let/let, cost/cost
Six of them cover most of what you will say: went, had, said, made, took, got
form.negative: did not go / didn't go — the special past word disappears and did carries the past instead
form.question: Did you go ...? — the plain verb comes back for the same reason

right.role: the past word you have to learn

spec.caption: Nothing is added and nothing is spelled out. One word is exchanged for another.

worked_example.sentence: We ate at the stall by the fish market and paid four pounds each.
worked_example.why_this_form: Ate is the whole past of eat; there is nothing to add to it. Paid sits beside it doing the same job with a different shape.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Eat would leave the meal in the speaker's ordinary week, as something they do rather than something they did on one occasion.

notice_set.sentence: The bakery sold out before ten.
notice_set.question: Could you still buy bread there at eleven?
notice_set.why: Sold is the past of sell, and the sentence closes the morning's stock before eleven arrives.

notice_set.sentence: They put the vegetables outside every morning that summer.
notice_set.question: Is this about one morning or about a run of mornings?
notice_set.why: Put looks the same in both places. Every morning that summer is what tells you the rest.

notice_set.sentence: The café kept its old sign when the owners changed.
notice_set.question: Is the sign still up?
notice_set.why: Kept closes the keeping at the moment the owners changed. Anything after that is a different sentence.

notice_set.sentence: I made the same soup for a week and got very tired of it.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker still want that soup?
notice_set.why: Two swapped past words in one sentence, and the second one lands on the speaker's feelings at the end of that week.

notice_set.sentence: The market began at six and the traders left by two.
notice_set.question: How many separate events are being reported?
notice_set.why: Began and left are two closed events with a gap between them, and neither takes an ending.

teach.rule_line: Some verbs swap to a different word for the past. Learn them in small families.
teach.false_rule: That there is a pattern underneath, and that once you find it you will not need the list. There is no pattern. Learning the list is the work.

errors.wrong: We eated at the harbour café before the film.
errors.right: We ate at the harbour café before the film.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner applies the rule they were given, and the rule is a good one. It is simply not the rule this verb obeys, and nothing in the sentence warns them.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: eated becomes ate.

errors.wrong: She buyed the bread from the stall at the end of the row.
errors.right: She bought the bread from the stall at the end of the row.
errors.why_it_happens: Buy sounds regular and looks regular. The past word shares almost no letters with it, so there is nothing to jog the memory in the middle of a sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: buyed becomes bought.

errors.wrong: The café opened at six and we come in for breakfast every morning of that week.
errors.right: The café opened at six and we came in for breakfast every morning of that week.
errors.why_it_happens: Come and came differ by one letter and the base form already sounds finished, so the ear accepts it. Habit words like every morning make it worse.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: come becomes came.

errors.wrong: He putted the tray down on the counter and went back for the rest.
errors.right: He put the tray down on the counter and went back for the rest.
errors.why_it_happens: A past with no visible mark feels unfinished, so the learner adds one to be safe. Adding it is the error the safety produces.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete three letters: putted becomes put.

pays_in.note: The verbs that carry a spoken story are almost all on this list.
pays_in.model: I took the coast road, got there far too early and sat outside for an hour.

pays_in.note: One wrong past word in an example is the most visible slip on the page.
pays_in.model: When the council brought the market indoors, the number of stalls fell by half.

pays_in.note: Some of these differ from their plain form by a single vowel and go past fast.
pays_in.model: They ran the stall for years and then sold it to a neighbour.

used_in.quote: A meal you enjoyed with other people is told with went, had, made, took and ate, and almost nothing else.
The passage narrates a stretch of the river's history, and the narration runs on these swapped past words.

payload.sentence: The stall sold out before the market closed.
payload.question: Was there anything left at the end?

feedback.why_key: Sold is the past of sell, and selling out empties the stall before the closing time arrives.
feedback.feed_forward: Recognise the past word first, then read what it claims.

payload.sentence: We put the chairs outside as soon as the rain stopped.
payload.question: Where does this sit?
options: a closed stretch of the past
something the speaker does every day

feedback.why_key: Put never changes shape, so the sentence next to it is what places the moment. Stopped has closed it.
feedback.feed_forward: When a verb never changes, read the verbs around it.

items.decision_cue: buyed the bread

payload.context: Idris is telling a friend about a morning at the market.
payload.sentence: I buyed the bread from the stall on the corner.
reasons: buy has its own past word and does not take the ending
bread cannot be bought at a stall
the speaker should be talking about today
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The rule is right and the verb is the exception. Buy exchanges itself for bought and takes nothing extra.
feedback.feed_forward: Check any verb you use often against the list before you trust the ending.

payload.context: Two friends talking about a meal at the harbour.
payload.stem: We ___ (eat) outside because the room upstairs was full.

feedback.why_key: Eat swaps to ate. Nothing is added and nothing is doubled.
feedback.feed_forward: Recall the past word before you reach for the ending.

payload.context: From a short piece about a market in Ashfield.
payload.stem: The council ___ (bring) the whole market indoors and half the traders left.

feedback.why_key: Bring belongs to the family that ends in ought: bring, buy, think and fight all land in the same place.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn this verb with the other ought verbs, not on its own.

payload.context: From a letter about a weekend away.
payload.stem: The cottage ___ (cost) less than the hotel and had a much better view.

feedback.why_key: Cost is one of the verbs that does nothing at all. Writing costed is the error that safety produces.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the do-nothing verbs alone: cut, put, let, cost.

payload.given: The owners take the tables in at six and the square goes quiet.
payload.instruction: Move the whole sentence into a summer that has ended.

expected: took the tables in at six and the square went quiet

feedback.why_key: Both verbs swap words rather than take endings, and the second one is the one people leave behind.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap every verb in the sentence, not the first.

payload.audio_text: They ran the stall for years and then sold it.

expected: they ran the stall for years and then sold it

feedback.why_key: Run and ran are one vowel apart, and at speed the vowel is the only evidence you get.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the vowel in the middle of short verbs.

payload.sentence: She putted the boxes down by the door and went to find a trolley.

feedback.why_key: Went is already right, so the sentence knows it is in the past. Put needs no help at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Take the ending off the do-nothing verbs.

items.decision_cue: we come in for rolls

payload.context: From a paragraph about a week spent working near the docks.
payload.sentence: The bakery started at five and we come in for rolls before every shift.
reasons: the second verb is still standing in the present
cafés do not open at six
the week is not named clearly enough
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Come and came are one letter apart, and the base form is quiet enough to slip past the writer's ear.
feedback.feed_forward: Check come, run and become twice; they hide well.

items.decision_cue: The kitchen cuts the bread each morning.

payload.context: Two lines from different notices in the same café.
sentences: The kitchen cuts the bread each morning.
The kitchen cut the bread each morning.
meanings: This is what happens here, and it will happen again tomorrow.
This is what used to happen during a stretch that has ended.

feedback.why_key: The verb never changes for the past, so the single letter on the present form is carrying the whole difference.
feedback.feed_forward: With do-nothing verbs, read the small letters closely.

payload.prompt_text: A meal you remember. Write one sentence using two of these verbs in the past: go, eat, take, buy, make, have.

points.title: Asking and denying things about the past without marking it twice

point_json.grammar_name: did in past questions and negatives

teach.can_do: I can ask about the past and say something did not happen, without marking the past twice.
teach.why_it_matters: Did you went is the most recognisable beginner error in English, and it survives to band six because nobody ever explains why did takes the past away from the main verb.
teach.meaning: English marks the past once per sentence and no more. In a plain statement the mark sits on the verb. The moment you ask a question or say something did not happen, the helper word did arrives and takes the mark with it. The main verb then goes back to the shape you would find in a dictionary. Nothing is lost: the past is still there, standing at the front of the sentence instead of in the middle.

form.pattern: did + the plain verb  (Did you go? · We did not go.)
notes: did and didn't never change: did I, did she, did they
didn't in speech and in a friendly message; did not in an essay
The plain verb is the dictionary one: go, buy, walk — never went, bought, walked
In a question the helper comes first, then the person, then the plain verb
form.negative: did not / didn't + the plain verb
form.question: Did + person + the plain verb ...?

left.role: where the past sits in a statement

right.role: where it moves to once did arrives
right.text: Did we walk to the harbour?

spec.caption: The past does not disappear from the question. It moves to the front and lets the verb go plain.

worked_example.sentence: Did you speak to the site office about the noise?

worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Do you speak to the site office about the noise? asks whether that is something you generally do, not whether one conversation happened.

notice_set.why: It is a genuine question, and the helper at the front is what turns a report into one.

notice_set.why: Didn't cancels the hearing across the whole fortnight, and the plain verb after it is doing no other work.

notice_set.sentence: Do you write to them every month?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking about now or about a finished occasion?
notice_set.why: Do at the front keeps the question in the speaker's present. Only one letter separates it from a question about a closed occasion.

notice_set.sentence: She didn't say which building she meant.
notice_set.question: Do we know which building she meant?
notice_set.why: The helper carries the past and the cancelling; say stays plain and simply names the missing action.

notice_set.sentence: Did they put the notice up before the meeting?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker checking the timing of something?
notice_set.why: Put looks identical in every position, so the helper at the front is the only thing that shows the past at all.

teach.rule_line: Once did is in the sentence, the main verb goes back to its plain shape.
teach.false_rule: That a past question needs a past verb inside it. It already has one. Did is the past, and marking it a second time is the commonest slip in English.

errors.wrong: Did you went to the meeting at the depot?
errors.right: Did you go to the meeting at the depot?
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows the question is about the past and checks that the past is showing. It is showing, twice, and the second one is on the word that has already handed the job over.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: went becomes go.
errors.l1_note: Languages that mark the past on every verb in the sentence make this feel like the careful choice.

errors.wrong: She didn't wrote back until the following week.
errors.right: She didn't write back until the following week.
errors.why_it_happens: Didn't is stored as one unbreakable word, so its past half stops being visible and the learner marks the past again on the next verb along.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: wrote becomes write.

errors.wrong: Did the two lifts worked that morning?
errors.right: Did the two lifts work that morning?
errors.why_it_happens: The ending is the learner's proof to themselves that they have understood the question is about a finished morning. Removing it feels like removing the meaning.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two letters: worked becomes work.

errors.wrong: I rang the office twice and they don't answer.
errors.right: I rang the office twice and they didn't answer.
errors.why_it_happens: The cancelled half of a sentence often gets chosen last and gets no attention at all, so it defaults to the shape the learner uses most, which is the present one.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: don't becomes didn't.

points.title: Saying which past you mean, and putting the when-words where English keeps them

point_json.grammar_name: Past time markers: yesterday, last …, … ago, in 2016, when I was …

teach.can_do: I can say exactly which past stretch of time I am talking about, and put the words in the right place.
teach.why_it_matters: These words are the evidence a listener uses to place your story. Put one in the wrong slot and the sentence sounds translated rather than wrong.
teach.meaning: A when-word does not make a sentence past. The verb has already done that. What the when-word does is choose which finished stretch of time the sentence lands in: the day before today, a named year, a summer that has ended, or the age you were. It narrows a claim the verb has already made, and it is the reason two speakers can tell the same story about two different decades.

form.pattern: yesterday · last night · last summer · two years ago · in 2016 · when I was twelve
notes: ago always follows the amount and counts backwards from today: three weeks ago
last takes no the in front of it: last summer, not the last summer
in with a year or a month, on with a day, at with a clock time
The natural slot is the end of the sentence; the front is available for emphasis, with a comma
form.negative: I did not train at all last winter.
form.question: When did you last play a full match?

spec.caption: Each word picks a different closed stretch. None of them is doing the work of putting the sentence in the past.

worked_example.sentence: The club moved to the new ground three years ago.
worked_example.why_this_form: Ago counts backwards from today, so the reader can place the move without being told the year, and the amount has to come in front of it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: In three years counts forwards instead, and would put the move in a future the rest of the sentence cannot be reporting.

notice_set.sentence: The pool closed for repairs last winter.
notice_set.question: How long ago was the closing, roughly?
notice_set.why: Last plus a season points at the most recent one that has finished, so it is always inside the past year.

notice_set.sentence: We joined the running club four years ago.
notice_set.question: Does the counting start from today or from some other point?
notice_set.why: Ago measures backwards from the moment of speaking, which is why the number changes as the years pass.

notice_set.sentence: In 2016 the council rebuilt the changing rooms.
notice_set.question: Does the reader need to know today's date to place this?
notice_set.why: A named year is fixed. It says the same thing in any decade, which is why reports prefer it.

notice_set.sentence: When I was eleven I trained twice a week.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker say how old they are now?
notice_set.why: An age marks a stretch of the speaker's own life without saying anything about where they stand today.

notice_set.sentence: The match finished late and the team travelled back the same night.
notice_set.question: Is there any word here naming a date?
notice_set.why: No date is named and none is needed. The verbs alone are enough to place the whole thing behind us.

teach.rule_line: The verb carries the past; the when-words only say which past you mean.
teach.false_rule: That a past sentence needs a when-word to be correct. Most have none, and one in every sentence makes a paragraph read like a diary entry.

errors.wrong: I played yesterday two matches at the sports centre.
errors.right: I played two matches at the sports centre yesterday.
errors.why_it_happens: In many languages the when-word sits comfortably next to the verb. English keeps the verb and the thing it acts on welded together and sends the when-word to the end.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: yesterday goes to the end.
errors.l1_note: Very common where the writer's first language has freer word order.

errors.wrong: Ago two weeks the pitch was flooded and the game was called off.
errors.right: Two weeks ago the pitch was flooded and the game was called off.
errors.why_it_happens: Ago is learned as a word meaning in the past, so it gets used like one, standing at the front. It is not that kind of word: it is a measurement that follows its amount.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: ago goes after the amount.

errors.wrong: We trained the last summer with the harbour club.
errors.right: We trained last summer with the harbour club.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows a particular summer is meant and reaches for the word that usually points at a particular thing. Last is already doing that job on its own.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: the.

errors.wrong: Three years ago the club moves to the ground behind the station.
errors.right: Three years ago the club moved to the ground behind the station.
errors.why_it_happens: Once a date is on the page the writer feels the past has been announced, so the verb seems free to relax. The verb is where English keeps the past, and the date cannot cover for it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one letter: the s becomes a d.

points.title: Putting a past moment inside something that was already going on

teach.can_do: I can describe what was already going on when something else happened.
teach.why_it_matters: Without it every story is a flat list of events. This form is what lets a listener see the scene the events landed in.
teach.meaning: Was or were plus an -ing word takes an activity and stretches it across a piece of past time, so that other things can happen inside it. It does not tell you the activity finished — only that it was running while you were looking. That is why it is the form English reaches for when it wants to hand you a picture instead of a fact: somebody standing on a platform, rain falling, a queue not moving.

form.pattern: was / were + the -ing word  (was waiting · were queuing)
notes: One thing takes was; more than one, and you, take were
The -ing word is the same one you already use for what is happening now
A few verbs describe a state rather than an activity and stay out of this form: know, want, own, mean, believe
In speech was and were shrink to almost nothing and the -ing word carries the sound
form.negative: was not / wasn't + -ing  ·  were not / weren't + -ing
form.question: Were you + -ing ...?

marks.label: the moment that lands inside it

spec.caption: The bar is what this form draws. The cross is somebody else's sentence.

worked_example.sentence: The 7.40 was standing at the platform with its doors open.
worked_example.why_this_form: The sentence hands you a picture rather than an event. The train had not just arrived and had not yet left; it was simply there when you looked.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Stood would report it as one finished thing the train did, and would not put you on the platform looking at it at all.

notice_set.sentence: The barriers were closing as I reached the crossing.
notice_set.question: Were the barriers fully down when the speaker arrived?
notice_set.why: The form catches the movement halfway through, so the barriers are still on their way down.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody was checking tickets on the late train.
notice_set.question: What would you have seen if you had walked through the carriage?
notice_set.why: The form describes the state of the carriage across a stretch, not one moment of it.

notice_set.sentence: We were waiting on the wrong side of the station.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker say whether the train came?
notice_set.why: The waiting is a scene. Whether anything arrived is a separate sentence that has not been said.

notice_set.sentence: The lifts weren't working at Ashfield that week.
notice_set.question: Could a passenger use a lift on the Wednesday of that week?
notice_set.why: Stretching the fault across the week puts every day of it inside the sentence.

notice_set.sentence: I knew the driver from the depot.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker describing something they did, or something that was simply true?
notice_set.why: Knowing is not an activity you can be caught in the middle of, which is why English leaves this verb alone.

teach.rule_line: Was or were plus -ing paints what was already going on, not what happened.
teach.false_rule: That the -ing form means the action took a long time. It can last two seconds. It means you are watching it run, not counting it as done.

errors.wrong: I was knowing the driver from the depot.
errors.right: I knew the driver from the depot.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is setting a scene, and this is the scene-setting form, so it gets applied to everything in the scene — including the things that are simply true rather than going on.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: was knowing becomes knew.

errors.wrong: The bus was arriving at nine and we got on.
errors.right: The bus arrived at nine and we got on.
errors.why_it_happens: A named clock time feels like a scene, so the scene-setting form arrives with it. Arriving at a stated time is a single landing, not a stretch anything can happen inside.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: was arriving becomes arrived.

errors.wrong: We were wanting a later train, so we changed the booking.
errors.right: We wanted a later train, so we changed the booking.
errors.why_it_happens: Wanting feels like something going on inside you, and in a sense it is. English still files it with the states and keeps it out of this form.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: were wanting becomes wanted.

pays_in.note: The long turn needs a scene before it can have events in it.

pays_in.note: A background clause explains why the example that follows it happened at all.

points.title: Choosing between the event and the scene it happened inside

teach.can_do: I can decide whether to report an event or paint the scene it happened inside.
teach.why_it_matters: Both forms are correct English and you can already build both. What costs marks is choosing the wrong one, and it happens in every story anybody tells.
teach.meaning: These two forms do not describe different events. They describe the same event from two distances. The plain past treats it as a whole thing that landed and finished, so the story can move on to the next item. Was or were plus -ing holds the same thing open and unfinished, so that something else can happen inside it. Choose the first for what happened; choose the second for what was already going on when it happened.

form.pattern: the event: plain past  ·  the scene: was / were + -ing
notes: A chain of finished events is all plain past, one after another
The scene usually comes first and the event lands inside it
Two scenes can run side by side; two events cannot happen at once unless you say so
The state verbs stay out of the -ing form no matter which job they are doing

form.question: Did you check ...?  ·  Were you checking ...?

points.title: Saying that something was true for a stretch of the past and is not true now

point_json.grammar_name: used to, and how it differs from would and from the plain past

teach.can_do: I can say that something was the case for a stretch of the past and has since stopped.
teach.why_it_matters: There are three ways to talk about a past habit and they are not the same. Choosing between them is what makes an answer about your childhood sound like English rather than translation.
teach.meaning: Used to makes two claims in three words. First, this was the case over a stretch of past time, not on one occasion. Second, it has stopped. The second claim is the one nobody teaches and the one that does the work: the moment you say used to, your listener understands that things are different now. If that is not what you mean, this is not the phrase you want.

form.pattern: used to + the plain verb  (used to live · used to walk · there used to be)
notes: The d is silent in speech, so it sounds like use to — but it is written used to
After did the d comes off: didn't use to, did you use to
Would plus the plain verb can do repeated actions once the past scene is already set, and it reads as fond or reflective
Would cannot carry a state: there would be a ferry is not an option, and this rule decides most cases
form.negative: did not use to / didn't use to + the plain verb
form.question: Did you use to + the plain verb ...?

points.title: Telling a past story in an order a listener can follow

point_json.grammar_name: Narrative sequence: the past chain and its joining words

teach.can_do: I can tell a past story so that a listener always knows which part came first.
teach.why_it_matters: The two-minute long turn is a narrative task. A story told out of order costs marks nobody will ever explain to you, because the listener simply stops following.
teach.meaning: A story is a chain: finished event, finished event, finished event, told in the order they happened. The plain past carries the chain, one link at a time. The held-open form drops in wherever you want the listener to see the scene rather than the next step, and the joining words tell them where they are standing. Change nothing about the verbs and the order still works, because English trusts the order of the sentences.

form.pattern: plain past + plain past + plain past, with the joining words between
notes: First, After that and In the end open a sentence and take a comma
While plus was or were plus -ing gives the scene the next event lands in
Keep the events in the order they happened unless you say plainly that you are jumping back
Two or three joining words in a whole story is plenty; one on every sentence reads like a recipe
form.negative: did not tell the rest of it until later
form.question: What happened after that?

spec.caption: Three crosses in a row are the chain. The bar underneath them is the scene they happened in.

worked_example.sentence: We reached the square at seven, found a place near the railings and waited for the procession.
worked_example.why_this_form: Three finished steps in the order they happened, joined without fuss. The listener never has to work out what followed what.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Were reaching, were finding and were waiting would turn all three steps into scenery, and the listener would still be waiting for the story to begin.

notice_set.sentence: The drummers started, the lights went down and the crowd went quiet.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Nothing tells you the order except the order, and in a chain of finished steps that is enough.

notice_set.sentence: The square was filling up while we looked for a place at the front.
notice_set.question: Was the square empty when they arrived?
notice_set.why: The filling is held open around the looking, so it was already under way before they got there.

notice_set.sentence: We got there late. The procession had passed an hour earlier.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Here the order of the sentences and the order of events come apart, and the second sentence has to say so.

notice_set.sentence: After that, nobody moved for twenty minutes.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you what came before it?
notice_set.why: A joining word points backwards without repeating anything, which is exactly why a story needs a few of them.

notice_set.sentence: In the end we walked home along the harbour.
notice_set.question: Is this near the start or near the finish of the story?
notice_set.why: Some joining words carry a position in the story as part of their meaning, and a listener uses them to know when to relax.

teach.rule_line: Keep the chain in the plain past and let the joining words carry the order.
teach.false_rule: That a story sounds livelier told in the held-open form. A story told entirely in it has scenery on every side and no events anywhere.

errors.wrong: The procession finished and after that everybody was going home.
errors.right: The procession finished and after that everybody went home.
errors.why_it_happens: The last step of a story often gets stretched for effect, as if a slow ending were a better one. It stops the chain from closing and leaves the listener waiting.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: was going becomes went.

errors.wrong: The drummers started, the lights went down and the crowd goes quiet.
errors.right: The drummers started, the lights went down and the crowd went quiet.
errors.why_it_happens: The last link in a chain is chosen when the writer is already thinking about the next sentence, and it defaults to the shape they use most often.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: goes becomes went.

errors.wrong: We arrived at the hall, and after that everybody is finding a seat.
errors.right: We arrived at the hall, and after that everybody found a seat.
errors.why_it_happens: The joining word feels as if it has already done the work of placing the sentence in time, so the verb is left to look after itself and does not.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is finding becomes found.

pays_in.note: The whole long turn is this, from the first sentence to the last.
pays_in.model: We got there at six, waited near the railings and left before the crowd did.

pays_in.note: An example is a small story, and it fails if the order fails.
pays_in.model: The council trialled the scheme for a year, published the figures and quietly dropped it.

pays_in.note: Ordering questions turn on the joining words rather than on the events.
pays_in.model: After that the group moved to the second hall, and the talk started twenty minutes late.

items.decision_cue: the crowd goes quiet

payload.context: Somebody telling the story of an evening at a street festival.
payload.sentence: The band came on, the doors closed and the crowd goes quiet.
reasons: the last link in the chain has slipped into the present
the doors should not have closed
the crowd went quiet too early
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two links are closed and the third is not, so the story stops being a story halfway through the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the last verb of every chain you write.

payload.context: From an account of an evening at the arts centre in Verdon.
payload.stem: We reached the hall at seven and ___ (find) a seat near the back.

feedback.why_key: Two finished steps in a row, so the second one closes exactly as the first did.
feedback.feed_forward: Match every link in the chain to the one before it.

payload.context: From the same account, three sentences later.
payload.stem: The hall ___ (fill) up while the first group tuned their instruments.

feedback.why_key: This one is the scene rather than a step, and the tuning is what happens inside it.
feedback.feed_forward: Hold the scene open and close the steps.

payload.context: Build the next sentence of a story that already has two steps in it.

expected: after that the procession turned into the harbour road

feedback.why_key: The joining word opens the sentence and points backwards without repeating a word of what came before.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the joining word, then give the next step.

payload.given: The rain started. We were standing at the front of the crowd.
payload.instruction: Join these into one sentence in which the standing is the scene and the rain is the event.

expected: were standing at the front of the crowd when the rain started
were standing at the front of the crowd when it started to rain

feedback.why_key: The scene has to be open for the event to land in it, and putting the scene first is what tells a listener which is which.
feedback.feed_forward: Scene first, then the event that lands in it.

payload.audio_text: After that we walked home and nobody said much.

expected: after that we walked home and nobody said much

feedback.why_key: The ending on the first verb is a single consonant at speed, and it is the only thing keeping the sentence in the story.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the ending you heard, not the one you expected.

items.decision_cue: everybody is finding a seat

payload.context: From the middle of a story about a village hall meeting.
payload.sentence: We arrived at the hall, and after that everybody is finding a seat.
reasons: the joining word cannot place the sentence in time on its own
the meeting was not in a hall
arriving and sitting down are the same step
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The joining word points backwards but it does not carry the past. Only the verb can do that.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the verb yourself; the joining word will not.

payload.sentence: The procession finished and after that everybody was going home.

feedback.why_key: The last step of a story has to close, or the listener is left standing in the square waiting for the rest.
feedback.feed_forward: Close the final step of every story.

items.decision_cue: We got to the square and the procession passed.

payload.context: Two versions of the same evening, written by two people who were there.
sentences: We got to the square and the procession passed.
We got to the square. The procession had passed an hour earlier.
meanings: They arrived first and saw the procession go by afterwards.
They missed it: the procession was over before they arrived.

feedback.why_key: In the first, the order of the sentences is the order of events. In the second, the writer has to say plainly that it is not.
feedback.feed_forward: Say so explicitly whenever you jump backwards.

parts: The first speaker arrived twenty minutes late.
model_combinations: The hall was filling up slowly when the first speaker arrived twenty minutes late, and nobody complained.
The hall filled up slowly, the first speaker arrived twenty minutes late and nobody complained about the delay.
While the hall was still filling up, the first speaker arrived twenty minutes late, and not one person complained.

feedback.why_key: One of the three facts is the scene and the other two are steps, and choosing which is which is the whole task.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide which fact is the scene, then chain the rest.

payload.prompt_text: An occasion you took part in. Write three short sentences telling what happened, in order, with one joining word and no more.

feedback.why_key: Three closed steps and one signpost is the whole shape of a spoken story, and adding more signposts makes it worse rather than clearer.
feedback.feed_forward: Use one joining word; let the order do the rest.

payload.prompt_text: You have two minutes on the card A time you took part in a traditional occasion. One scene at the start, then a chain of closed steps, then a closed ending. Two joining words at most. One minute to plan.

feedback.why_key: This is the task the whole unit has been building towards: a scene, a chain and an ending that actually ends.
feedback.feed_forward: Plan three steps before you start speaking.
